claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined genetic, cellular, and mouse model data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The neuroendocrine cellular compartment is implicated in IBD.
claims.source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that functional deficiency in SCGN can result in intestinal inflammation and implicates the neuroendocrine cellular compartment in IBD.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing SCGN expression in neuroendocrine cells and the colitis phenotype in deficient models.

claims.claim: Twin concordance studies were the first to recognize the contribution of genetic factors to IBD pathogenesis.
claims.source: Twin concordance studies were the first to recognize the contribution of genetic factors to IBD pathogenesis (Brant, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brant, 2011.

claims.claim: Over 200 variants associated with genetic risk for IBD have been identified through genome-wide association studies.
claims.source: At the present time, a series of large genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified over 200 variants associated with genetic risk (Liu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Most GWAS-identified IBD risk variants are intergenic and confer only modest risk with odds ratios typically below 2.
claims.source: Most of these variants are intergenic and confer only modest risk (with odds ratios typically below 2).
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about GWAS findings in IBD.

claims.claim: Over 50 genes have been linked to early-onset IBD in pediatric populations.
claims.source: Studies in pediatric populations have focused on monogenic Mendelian traits and have identified over 50 genes that can be linked to early-onset IBD (Uhlig and Schwerd, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Uhlig and Schwerd, 2016.

claims.claim: The vast majority of early-onset IBD mutations result in complex syndromes of immune dysfunction or developmental alterations that resemble only in part the phenotype of adult-onset IBD.
claims.source: Interestingly, the vast majority of these mutations result in complex syndromes of immune dysfunction or developmental alterations that resemble only in part the phenotype of adult-onset IBD.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about monogenic IBD.

claims.claim: The identified IBD loci contribute to about 20–30% of the genetic risk.
claims.source: In aggregate, the identified loci contribute to about 20–30% of the genetic risk, highlighting the need for additional gene discovery.
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the explained heritability of IBD.

claims.claim: The luminal aspect of the intestine represents the largest epithelial surface in the body.
claims.source: This is likely the case because the luminal aspect of the intestine represents the largest epithelial surface in the body (Furness et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Furness et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The intestine houses the largest concentration of human-associated microbiota.
claims.source: and houses the largest concentration of human-associated microbiota (Li et al., 2014a; Qin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2014a and Qin et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The intestine contains the greatest number of immune cells in the body.
claims.source: As such, it is not surprising that the intestine contains the greatest number of immune cells in the body (Castro and Arntzen, 1993)
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castro and Arntzen, 1993.

claims.claim: EECs comprise 1% of the intestinal epithelium.
claims.source: EECs comprise 1% of the intestinal epithelium and in aggregate represent the largest endocrine cell population in the body (Sternini et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sternini et al., 2008.

claims.claim: EECs in aggregate represent the largest endocrine cell population in the body.
claims.source: EECs comprise 1% of the intestinal epithelium and in aggregate represent the largest endocrine cell population in the body (Sternini et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sternini et al., 2008.

claims.claim: EECs secrete peptide hormones in response to nutrients or other small molecules.
claims.source: These cells secrete peptide hormones in response to nutrients or other small molecules, which are recognized by specific cell surface receptors often located on the luminal membrane.
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about EEC function.

claims.claim: Most secreted products produced by EECs are involved in regulating the digestive process, gastrointestinal motility, and the metabolic adaptation to nutrient influx.
claims.source: Most secreted products produced by EECs are involved in regulating the digestive process, gastrointestinal motility, and the metabolic adaptation to nutrient influx (Drucker, 2007; Murphy and Bloom, 2006; Rindi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Drucker, 2007; Murphy and Bloom, 2006; Rindi et al., 2004.

claims.claim: There are more than 10 distinct populations of EECs with distinct hormone secretory characteristics in the small intestine based on gene expression profiling.
claims.source: Based on gene expression profiling, there are more than 10 distinct populations of EECs with distinct hormone secretory characteristics in the small intestine (Furness et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Furness et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Human mutations impacting NEUROG3 have been described in patients with chronic diarrhea secondary to malabsorption without an inflammatory component.
claims.source: Notably, human mutations impacting NEUROG3, the transcription factor required for EEC differentiation, have been described in patients with chronic diarrhea secondary to malabsorption without an inflammatory component (Wang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Gut neurons are aggregated in two distinct locations in the intestinal wall: the submucosal plexus and the myenteric plexus.
claims.source: Another related cellular compartment is comprised of gut neurons, which are aggregated in two distinct locations in the intestinal wall: the submucosal plexus and the myenteric plexus.
claims.evidence: This reflects established anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: Gut neurons are derived from neural crest progenitors.
claims.source: Derived from neural crest progenitors, these cells are integral to the motility function of the gut
claims.evidence: This reflects established developmental biology knowledge.

claims.claim: Gut neurons interconnect with EECs and form a neuro-epithelial circuit that is ultimately connected to the central nervous system.
claims.source: In fact, recently, gut neurons were demonstrated to interconnect with EECs and form a neuro-epithelial circuit that is ultimately connected to the central nervous system (Kaelberer et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaelberer et al., 2018.

claims.claim: A consanguineous Hispanic family with three of five children affected by an aggressive form of early onset ulcerative colitis was identified.
claims.source: We identified a consanguineous Hispanic family with three of five children affected by an aggressive form of early onset ulcerative colitis (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clinical data and the pedigree shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: All three probands were diagnosed by standard clinical, endoscopic, and histologic criteria.
claims.source: All three probands were diagnosed by standard clinical, endoscopic, and histologic criteria (Levine et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clinical data and a citation to diagnostic criteria (Levine et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Siblings P1 and P2 were diagnosed at age eight.
claims.source: Two siblings (P1 and P2) were diagnosed at age eight
claims.evidence: This is clinical data from the patient records.

claims.claim: Sibling P3 was diagnosed at age 6.
claims.source: while the third (P3) was diagnosed at age 6.
claims.evidence: This is clinical data from the patient records.

claims.claim: Siblings P1 and P2 had a severe disease phenotype characterized by pancolonic involvement and anti-TNF treatment failure, ultimately requiring procto-colectomy.
claims.source: Siblings P1 and P2 had a severe disease phenotype characterized by pancolonic involvement, anti-TNF treatment failure, ultimately requiring procto-colectomy 9 years and 9 months after diagnosis, respectively (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by clinical data and endoscopic images in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Sibling P3 had a milder phenotype with exclusive rectal involvement, controlled on oral mesalamine.
claims.source: Sibling P3 had a milder phenotype with exclusive rectal involvement, controlled on oral mesalamine up until last point of follow up.
claims.evidence: This is clinical data from the patient records.

claims.claim: The consanguineous nature of the family pedigree suggested an autosomal recessive trait.
claims.source: The consanguineous nature of the family pedigree suggested an autosomal recessive trait, where each of the affected individuals inherited a recessive allele from one of their parents.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the pedigree structure and inheritance pattern.

claims.claim: Large segments of LOH on chromosomes 6 and 12 were shared between all three affected probands and not present in the unaffected siblings.
claims.source: Through this analysis, we identified large segments of LOH on chromosomes 6 and 12 that were shared between all three affected probands and not present in the unaffected siblings (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SNP array data presented in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: WES analysis identified a single rare (MAF <1%) homozygous missense variant in the SCGN gene (rs376721140; NM_006998.3:c.230G > A; p.Arg77His) that was shared by the three probands and not their unaffected siblings.
claims.source: WES analysis identified a single rare (MAF <1%) homozygous missense variant in the SCGN gene (rs376721140; NM_006998.3:c.230G > A; p.Arg77His) that was shared by the three probands and not their unaffected siblings.
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-exome sequencing data.

claims.claim: The SCGN variant mapped to one of the segments of shared LOH on chromosome 6.
claims.source: This variant mapped to one of the segments of shared LOH on chromosome 6.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic mapping data.

claims.claim: WGS confirmed that the SCGN variant is the only rare homozygous nonsynonymous candidate variant in the segments of shared LOH among the probands.
claims.source: WGS confirmed that the SCGN variant is the only rare homozygous nonsynonymous candidate variant in the segments of shared LOH among these probands.
claims.evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claims.claim: Familial segregation of the SCGN p.R77H mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, showing that both parents were heterozygote carriers.
claims.source: Finally, familial segregation of the SCGN p.R77H mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, showing that both parents were heterozygote carriers, and the unaffected siblings were either a heterozygote carrier or had reference alleles, as per WES results (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The allelic frequency for the SCGN p.R77H variant in ExAC is 0.014% overall and 0.017% in Hispanics.
claims.source: The allelic frequency for the variant found in affected individuals in this family is very rare (all ExAC = 0.014%; Hispanics only = 0.017%).
claims.evidence: This is data from the ExAC database.

claims.claim: The mutation frequency among Hispanics in the Dallas Heart Study was 0.025%.
claims.source: The mutation frequency among Hispanics in the Dallas Heart Study was 0.025%.
claims.evidence: This is supported by genotyping data from the Dallas Heart Study.

claims.claim: No homozygous individuals for the SCGN p.R77H variant were identified within the Dallas Heart Study or reported in public genomic databases.
claims.source: Furthermore, in agreement with the rarity of this allele, no homozygous individual were identified within the Dallas Heart Study nor reported in public genomic databases (ExAC; Lek et al., 2016), 1000 Genomes Project (1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015), dbSNP (National Center for Biotechnology Information, 2019) or IBD exomes browser (Inflammatory Bowel Disease Exomes Browser, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from multiple genomic databases.

claims.claim: Secretagogin is a calcium sensing protein predicted to have 6 EF–hand domains.
claims.source: Secretagogin, the protein encoded by the SCGN gene, is a calcium sensing protein predicted to have 6 EF–hand domains (Wagner et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wagner et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The identified variant (p.R77H) maps to a highly conserved Arginine in the predicted second EF hand of the protein.
claims.source: The identified variant (p.R77H) maps to a highly conserved Arginine in the predicted second EF hand of the protein, which is substituted for Histidine (Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: Arginine 77 exhibited limited coding variation in ExAC, consistent with a potentially important functional role for this residue.
claims.source: Arginine 77 exhibited limited coding variation, consistent with a potentially important functional role for this residue.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of ExAC allele frequency data shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: SCGN is expressed in scattered triangularly-shaped epithelial cells in rectal biopsies from healthy individuals, morphologically compatible with EECs.
claims.source: We performed immunohistochemistry of rectal biopsies from healthy individuals and observed strong expression among scattered triangularly-shaped epithelial cells, morphologically compatible with EECs (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: The pattern and morphology of SCGN-expressing cells was not affected in colonic tissues from the probands.
claims.source: When colonic tissues from the probands (P1, P2 and P3) were stained, the pattern and morphology of these cells was not affected (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: SCGN co-stained with Chromogranin A in some cells in the mouse intestine, with greater co-staining in the colon than in the small bowel.
claims.source: We observed that SCGN was confined to rare cells that co-stained in some instances for Chromogranin A (CGA), a marker of certain EEC populations (Figure 2c), with the degree of costaining being greater in the mouse colon, and minimal in the mouse small bowel (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2c and 2d.

claims.claim: In human colonic tissues, SCGN co-localized with other EEC markers such as Chromogranin B, Serotonin and glucagon in a subpopulation of cells.
claims.source: Similar findings were made in human colonic tissues, where in a subpopulation of cells, SCGN co-localized with other EEC markers such as Chromogranin B (CGB), Serotonin (5-HT) and glucagon (GCG) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: SCGN marks a unique sub-population of EECs, in agreement with single-cell expression profiling of the murine small intestinal epithelium.
claims.source: These findings suggested that SCGN marks a unique sub-population of EECs, in agreement with recent single-cell expression profiling of the murine small intestinal epithelium, which identified Scgn as a marker of a specific small intestinal EEC population (Haber et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data in the manuscript and a citation to Haber et al., 2017.

claims.claim: SCGN positive cells in the submucosal and muscle layers of the murine intestine co-stained for neuronal markers TUJ1, SNAP25 and synaptophysin.
claims.source: In addition, distinct clusters of SCGN positive cells in the submucosal and muscle layers of the murine intestine also co-stained for the neuronal markers TUJ1, SNAP25 and synaptophysin (SYP), consistent with SCGN expression in subpopulations of gut neurons (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: SCGN protein expression was uniform in murine pancreatic islets where it colocalized with CGA.
claims.source: In contrast with the partial overlap seen in intestinal tissues between SCGN and EEC or neuronal markers, SCGN protein expression was uniform in murine pancreatic islets where it colocalized with CGA (Figure 2f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2f.

claims.claim: SCGN interacts with the SNARE complex components SNAP23 and SNAP25.
claims.source: Previous studies have identified that SCGN interacts with the SNARE complex components SNAP23 and SNAP25, suggesting that this factor regulates neurotransmitter and hormone release in cells that express SCGN (Bauer et al., 2011; Rogstam et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bauer et al., 2011 and Rogstam et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Two independent Scgn knockout clones displayed loss of protein expression.
claims.source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology to target the first exon of murine Scgn, we generated two independent Scgn knockout (KO) clones that displayed loss of protein expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Lack of SCGN expression led to a significant decline in GLP-1 secretion when compared to parental cell lines.
claims.source: Lack of SCGN expression led to a significant decline in GLP-1 secretion when compared to parental cell lines, indicating that SCGN is required for optimal DHA-stimulated GLP-1 secretion from cultured EECs (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GLP-1 secretion assay data shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: DHA stimulated GLP-1 secretion was significantly impaired in cells expressing SCGNR77H compared to the isogenic wild-type control cells.
claims.source: DHA stimulated GLP-1 secretion was significantly impaired in cells expressing SCGNR77H compared to the isogenic wild-type control cells (Figure 3b), suggesting that the disease-associated variant is a hypomorphic allele that leads to altered secretion dynamics in EECs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GLP-1 secretion assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: The disease-associated SCGN variant is a hypomorphic allele that leads to altered secretion dynamics in EECs.
claims.source: DHA stimulated GLP-1 secretion was significantly impaired in cells expressing SCGNR77H compared to the isogenic wild-type control cells (Figure 3b), suggesting that the disease-associated variant is a hypomorphic allele that leads to altered secretion dynamics in EECs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the GLP-1 secretion data shown in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Immunoprecipitation of SCGN from STC-1 cells expressing either WT or the R77H variants led to comparable co-precipitation of endogenous SNAP25.
claims.source: Immunoprecipitation of SCGN from STC-1 cells expressing either WT or the R77H variants led to comparable co-precipitation of endogenous SNAP25 from these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In parental STC-1 cells, both SCGN and SNAP25 displayed vesicular and plasma membrane localization.
claims.source: In parental STC-1 cells, both SCGN and SNAP25 displayed vesicular and plasma membrane localization (Figure 3c, left column).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: The membranous localization of SNAP25 was lost in Scgn KO cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, the membranous localization of SNAP25 was lost in Scgn KO cells (Figure 3c, EV lane)
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Normal cellular localization of SNAP25 is dependent on the expression of its partner SCGN.
claims.source: and this was restored upon re-expression of SCGNWT (Figure 3c), indicating that normal cellular localization of SNAP25 is dependent on the expression of its partner SCGN.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: SCGNR77H failed to restore SNAP25 plasma membrane localization.
claims.source: In contrast, SCGNR77H failed to restore SNAP25 plasma membrane localization (Figure 3c, right column), and these distribution changes were highly significant after image quantification (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c and quantification in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: SCGNR77H itself also failed to localize to the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Consistent with its role in directing membrane localization of SNAP25, SCGNR77H itself also failed to localize to the plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This is based on the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: SCGNR77H displays abnormal subcellular localization which also impacts its partner, SNAP25, ultimately resulting in altered SNARE function and vesicular secretion.
claims.source: In aggregate, these observations indicate that SCGNR77H displays abnormal subcellular localization which also impact its partner, SNAP25, ultimately resulting in altered SNARE function and vesicular secretion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Figure 3.

claims.claim: The zebrafish SCGN ortholog is 73% identical to the human protein.
claims.source: To determine whether SCGN p.R77H also behaved as a loss of function allele in vivo, we investigated the function of SCGN in zebrafish, whose ortholog is 73% identical to the human protein.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data.

claims.claim: SCGN suppression using a translation blocking morpholino led to reduced midbrain size in zebrafish.
claims.source: SCGN suppression using a translation blocking morpholino (MO) targeting the ATG start codon led to the expected developmental phenotype of reduced midbrain size (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The reduced midbrain phenotype in zebrafish was rescued when human SCGNWT mRNA was co-injected.
claims.source: Importantly, this phenotype was rescued when human SCGNWT mRNA was co-injected
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Co-injection of mRNA encoding the R77H mutant failed to rescue the reduced midbrain phenotype in zebrafish.
claims.source: whereas co-injection of mRNA encoding the R77H mutant failed to rescue the phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: SCGNR77H is devoid of normal activity in cellular and in vivo developmental models.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings are consistent with SCGNR77H being devoid of normal activity in cellular and in vivo developmental models.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Figure 3.

claims.claim: Two independent founder lineages of Scgn knockout mice were selected (Secret1 and Secret2), each with Scgn deletions.
claims.source: Two independent founder lineages were selected (Secret1 and Secret2), each with Scgn deletions that could be easily detected by PCR-based genotyping (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claims.claim: Homozygous Secret1 and Secret2 mice expressed a truncated transcript skipping exon 3 of the gene.
claims.source: Homozygous Secret1 and Secret2 mice expressed a truncated transcript skipping exon 3 of the gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence staining demonstrated loss of SCGN protein expression in Secret1 and Secret2 mouse lines.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence staining and imaging of pancreatic islets using an antibody to an epitope not affected by the observed exon skipping demonstrated loss of SCGN protein expression in these two mouse lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claims.claim: At baseline, Scgn deficient mice did not develop any overt phenotype.
claims.source: At baseline, Scgn deficient mice (Secret1 and Secret2) did not develop any overt phenotype, including no obvious architectural abnormality in the colonic epithelium as seen in HE or alcian blue staining (Figure 4a), and no colitis was noted clinically or histologically even in mice as old as 330 days.
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4a and clinical observations.

claims.claim: Key markers of specialized epithelial populations remained intact in Scgn deficient mice.
claims.source: Gene expression analyses indicated that key markers of specialized epithelial populations remained intact in these mice (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: Bacterial diversity and microbiota composition were not significantly different between WT and homozygous Secret1 mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, bacterial diversity and microbiota composition were not significantly different between WT and homozygous Secret1 mice (Figure 4c–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4c–e.

claims.claim: Homozygous Secret1 male mice experienced worse weight loss upon administration of DSS.
claims.source: Upon administration of DSS, homozygous Secret1 male mice experienced worse weight loss (Figure 5a)
claims.evidence: This is supported by weight loss data shown in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: Homozygous Secret1 male mice had elevated disease activity index upon administration of DSS.
claims.source: elevated disease activity index (Figure 5b)
claims.evidence: This is supported by disease activity index data shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: Homozygous Secret1 male mice had greater mortality upon administration of DSS.
claims.source: greater mortality (Figure 5c)
claims.evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: Homozygous Secret1 male mice had increased tissue damage by histopathology upon administration of DSS.
claims.source: and increased tissue damage by histopathology (Figure 5d,e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5d,e.

claims.claim: Greater weight loss in DSS-treated mice was recapitulated when performing experiments without gender selection.
claims.source: Greater weight loss was also recapitulated when performing these experiments without gender selection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a)
claims.evidence: This is supported by weight loss data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Greater weight loss in DSS-treated mice was also seen in the Secret2 line.
claims.source: and was also seen in the Secret2 line (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by weight loss data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Loss of Scgn led to increased expression of pro-inflammatory genes in colonic tissues in Secret1 homozygous mice.
claims.source: In agreement with the more severe colitis in Scgn knockout mice, loss of Scgn led to increased expression of pro-inflammatory genes in colonic tissues in Secret1 (Figure 5f)
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: Loss of Scgn led to increased expression of pro-inflammatory genes in colonic tissues in Secret2 homozygous mice.
claims.source: and Secret2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) homozygous mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: Loss of Scgn in mice results in increased susceptibility to colitis.
claims.source: In aggregate, the data indicate that loss of Scgn in mice results in increased susceptibility to colitis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined DSS colitis data from Figure 5.

claims.claim: Flow cytometric analysis of colonic and small bowel lamina propria leukocyte populations from WT and Secret1 animals showed no differences in populations of cell types examined.
claims.source: Flow cytometric analysis of colonic and small bowel lamina propria leukocyte populations from WT and Secret1 animals showed no differences in populations of cell types examined (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Neurog3 deletion in the colonic epithelium was accomplished using a colonocyte-specific CDX2-Cre transgene.
claims.source: Neurog3 deletion in the colonic epithelium was accomplished using a colonocyte-specific transgene (Hinoi et al., 2007), CDX2-Cre (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the breeding strategy shown in Figure 6a and a citation to Hinoi et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Neurog3ΔCol mice lost all CGA positive cells in the colonic epithelium, while showing no changes in the small intestine.
claims.source: The resulting mice lost all CGA positive cells in the colonic epithelium, while showing no changes in the small intestine (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: Gene expression of EEC-specific genes such as Neurog3 and Gcg was lost from colonocytes in Neurog3ΔCol mice.
claims.source: Gene expression of EEC-specific genes such as Neurog3 and Gcg was lost from colonocytes, while goblet cell markers were unaffected (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: Ablation of EECs in the colon led to loss of Scgn expression in this compartment.
claims.source: Importantly, ablation of EECs in the colon led to loss of Scgn expression in this compartment as would be expected (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: RNA sequencing analysis indicated that colonic Neurog3 deficiency was associated with loss of predicted or known EEC transcripts, including Scgn.
claims.source: Moreover, RNA sequencing analysis from colonocyte isolates also indicated that colonic Neurog3 deficiency was associated with loss of predicted or known EEC transcripts, including Scgn (Figure 6d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: Colons from Neurog3ΔCol mice exhibited drastic loss of hormone secretion at baseline.
claims.source: Functionally, colons from these animals exhibited drastic loss of hormone secretion at baseline, as measured by ex-vivo colonic GLP-1 and GLP-2 secretion in organ cultures.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex-vivo secretion assay data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: DHA stimulation led to GLP-1 and GLP-2 release from EEC sufficient (Neurog3f/f) colon explants, but not from colons of EEC ablated (Neurog3ΔCol) littermates.
claims.source: Furthermore, DHA stimulation led to GLP-1 and GLP-2 release from EEC sufficient (Neurog3f/f) colon explants, but not from colons of EEC ablated (Neurog3ΔCol) littermates.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex-vivo secretion assay data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: GLP-1 and GLP-2 release in response to DHA was completely blunted in colon explants from Secret1 homozygous animals.
claims.source: In addition, GLP-1 and GLP-2 release in response to DHA was completely blunted in colon explants from Secret1 homozygous animals, consistent with the role of SCGN in this response (Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex-vivo secretion assay data shown in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: EEC deficient mice did not have increased susceptibility to DSS-induced colitis.
claims.source: Importantly, EEC deficient mice did not have increased susceptibility to DSS-induced colitis (Figure 6f,g)
claims.evidence: This is supported by DSS colitis data shown in Figure 6f,g.

claims.claim: Colonic EECs do not mediate the immunomodulatory effects of SCGN.
claims.source: suggesting that colonic EECs do not mediate the immunomodulatory effects of SCGN and raising the possibility that SCGN-expressing enteric neurons may modulate intestinal immune homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that EEC-deficient mice do not show increased colitis susceptibility.

claims.claim: SCGN-expressing enteric neurons may modulate intestinal immune homeostasis.
claims.source: suggesting that colonic EECs do not mediate the immunomodulatory effects of SCGN and raising the possibility that SCGN-expressing enteric neurons may modulate intestinal immune homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the elimination of colonic EECs as the relevant cell type.

claims.claim: The patients with SCGN mutations did not display any other clinically overt phenotypes outside of colitis.
claims.source: In contrast to other forms of monogenic IBD, which frequently involve other significant phenotypes in addition to intestinal inflammation (e.g., immunodeficiency, gut developmental problems, etc.), our patients did not display any other clinically overt phenotypes outside of colitis.
claims.evidence: This is based on clinical observations of the patients.

claims.claim: Mutations in STXBP2 can lead to altered NK cell degranulation, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and colitis.
claims.source: Interestingly, mutations in other regulators of the SNARE complex, namely STXBP2, can lead to altered NK cell degranulation, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and colitis (Meeths et al., 2010).

claims.claim: The fasting glycemia of the patients with SCGN mutations has been normal.
claims.source: For example, in contrast to the age-dependent onset of diabetes mellitus previously reported in Scgn-deficient mice (Malenczyk et al., 2017), the fasting glycemia of these patients has been normal, which is remarkable considering that they have been exposed, at times, to glucocorticoids.

claims.source: Similarly, the patients do not display any overt neurocognitive phenotypes, again in contrast with data from zebrafish and murine models of Scgn deficiency (Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2015; Hanics et al., 2017).

results.result: The manuscript provides background on IBD genetics, noting that IBD affects 1.5-3 million people in the US, is genetically determined with over 200 GWAS-identified risk variants (mostly intergenic with modest effect), and over 50 genes linked to early-onset IBD, yet 20-30% of genetic risk remains unexplained.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C11-C16 provide well-established background information about IBD epidemiology and genetics, supported by appropriate citations and general knowledge. These contextual claims are accurate and properly referenced.

results.result: The manuscript describes the intestinal environment and specialized cell populations, including that the intestine has the largest epithelial surface and microbiota concentration, contains the most immune cells, and houses enteroendocrine cells (EECs, 1% of epithelium) and gut neurons that form neuro-epithelial circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C28 provide established background on intestinal anatomy, cell populations, and their functions, all supported by appropriate citations. This contextual information is well-documented in the literature.

results.result: A consanguineous Hispanic family was identified with three of five children affected by early-onset ulcerative colitis, diagnosed at ages 6-8 by standard criteria, with two siblings showing severe pancolonic disease requiring colectomy and one showing milder rectal disease controlled by mesalamine.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 describe the clinical presentation of the index family, supported by clinical data, pedigree information (Figure 1a), endoscopic images (Figure 1b), and clinical timeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The clinical characterization is well-documented.

results.result: Genetic analysis identified a homozygous SCGN p.R77H variant (rs376721140; NM_006998.3:c.230G>A) segregating with disease in the family, located in shared LOH regions on chromosome 6, confirmed as the only rare homozygous nonsynonymous variant in LOH segments by WES and WGS, with proper familial segregation validated by Sanger sequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 describe the genetic discovery process using SNP arrays, WES, WGS, and Sanger sequencing. The data are presented in Table 1, Figure 1a, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The multi-platform approach and segregation analysis provide strong evidence for the variant identification.

results.result: The SCGN p.R77H variant is ultra-rare with allele frequencies of 0.014% (ExAC overall), 0.017% (ExAC Hispanics), and 0.025% (Dallas Heart Study Hispanics), with no homozygous individuals identified in any database.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 document the rarity of the variant using multiple population databases. The frequencies are consistent with a rare recessive disease allele, and the absence of homozygotes in large databases supports pathogenicity.

results.result: The SCGN p.R77H variant affects a highly conserved arginine at position 77 in the predicted second EF-hand domain of secretagogin (a calcium-sensing protein with 6 EF-hand domains), and this residue shows limited coding variation in ExAC, suggesting functional importance.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1c), allele frequency analysis (Figure 1d), and citation to Wagner et al., 2000. The conservation analysis and low allelic variation support potential functional significance of the affected residue.

results.result: SCGN is expressed in scattered triangularly-shaped epithelial cells (morphologically compatible with EECs) in human rectal biopsies, with expression pattern unchanged in patient tissues. In mouse intestine, SCGN partially co-localizes with EEC markers (CGA, CGB, 5-HT, GCG) marking a unique EEC subpopulation, and is also expressed in gut neurons co-staining with neuronal markers (TUJ1, SNAP25, SYP). In pancreatic islets, SCGN shows uniform expression with complete CGA co-localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 describe SCGN expression patterns supported by immunohistochemistry (Figure 2a-b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 2c-f, Figure 2—figure supplements 2-3). The morphometric quantification (Figure 2d) and citation to Haber et al., 2017 support the characterization of SCGN-expressing cell populations.

results.result: SCGN interacts with SNARE complex components SNAP23 and SNAP25. CRISPR/Cas9-generated Scgn knockout STC-1 cell clones showed significantly reduced DHA-stimulated GLP-1 secretion compared to parental cells, and cells expressing SCGNR77H showed significantly impaired GLP-1 secretion compared to wild-type SCGN rescue, indicating the variant is a hypomorphic allele affecting secretion dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by citations (Bauer et al., 2011; Rogstam et al., 2007), western blot validation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and GLP-1 secretion assays (Figure 3a-b). The functional data demonstrate both loss of SCGN and the R77H variant impair hormone secretion, though statistical significance is shown.

results.result: SCGNR77H retains binding to SNAP25 by co-immunoprecipitation but fails to properly localize SNAP25 to the plasma membrane. In parental cells, both SCGN and SNAP25 show vesicular and plasma membrane localization, but SNAP25 membrane localization is lost in Scgn KO cells and restored by wild-type SCGN but not by SCGNR77H. The R77H variant itself also fails to localize to the plasma membrane, indicating abnormal subcellular localization affecting SNAP25 and ultimately SNARE function.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and immunofluorescence imaging with quantification (Figure 3c-d). The data demonstrate that while protein-protein interaction is maintained, subcellular localization is disrupted, providing a mechanistic explanation for functional impairment.

results.result: In zebrafish (73% identical ortholog), SCGN suppression by morpholino caused reduced midbrain size, which was rescued by human SCGNWT mRNA but not by SCGNR77H mRNA, demonstrating that SCGNR77H is devoid of normal activity in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing the developmental phenotype and differential rescue by wild-type versus mutant SCGN. This provides in vivo validation that R77H is a loss-of-function allele.

results.result: Two independent Scgn knockout mouse lines (Secret1 and Secret2) were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 targeting exon 3, resulting in truncated transcripts and loss of SCGN protein expression. At baseline, Scgn-deficient mice showed no overt phenotype, normal colonic architecture, intact epithelial cell markers, and no differences in microbiota diversity or composition compared to wild-type mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by genotyping data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b), RT-PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d), immunofluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e), histology (Figure 4a), qRT-PCR (Figure 4b), and 16S rRNA sequencing (Figure 4c-e). The baseline characterization is thorough and well-documented.

results.result: Upon DSS administration, Scgn-deficient mice (Secret1 and Secret2 lines) showed increased susceptibility to colitis with worse weight loss, elevated disease activity index, greater mortality, increased histological damage, and elevated pro-inflammatory gene expression compared to wild-type mice. This phenotype was observed in male-only and mixed-gender cohorts and in both independent knockout lines. Baseline lamina propria leukocyte populations showed no differences between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C86 are supported by weight loss data (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b), disease activity index (Figure 5b), survival curves (Figure 5c), histological scoring (Figure 5d-e), and qRT-PCR of inflammatory markers (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c). Flow cytometry data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) show no baseline immune differences. The colitis phenotype is replicated across two independent lines and multiple experimental conditions.

results.result: Colonic EEC ablation was achieved using CDX2-Cre to delete Neurog3 in colonocytes, resulting in loss of CGA-positive cells and EEC-specific gene expression (including Scgn) in the colon but not small intestine, confirmed by immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and RNA-seq. Functionally, Neurog3ΔCol mice showed drastically reduced baseline and DHA-stimulated GLP-1 and GLP-2 secretion from colon explants, similar to the blunted response in Secret1 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 are supported by breeding strategy diagram (Figure 6a), immunofluorescence (Figure 6b), qRT-PCR (Figure 6c), RNA-seq heatmap (Figure 6d), and ex-vivo hormone secretion assays (Figure 6e). The EEC ablation model is well-characterized and functionally validated.

results.result: EEC-deficient (Neurog3ΔCol) mice did not show increased susceptibility to DSS-induced colitis, suggesting that colonic EECs do not mediate the immunomodulatory effects of SCGN and raising the possibility that SCGN-expressing enteric neurons may modulate intestinal immune homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by DSS colitis data (Figure 6f-g) showing no difference between Neurog3f/f and Neurog3ΔCol mice. This is a critical negative result that redirects the mechanistic interpretation from EECs to neurons. However, C97 is speculative and requires future validation with neuron-specific models.

results.result: The patients with SCGN mutations displayed only colitis without other clinically overt phenotypes (unlike other monogenic IBD forms), normal fasting glycemia (unlike Scgn-deficient mice that develop diabetes), and no neurocognitive phenotypes (unlike zebrafish/mouse models). SCGN protein is absent from the immune system, pointing to neuroendocrine cells as the source of pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are based on clinical observations and comparisons to other disease models and SCGN expression patterns. The citations to Malenczyk et al., 2017; Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2015; Hanics et al., 2017; and Meeths et al., 2010 support the comparisons. The phenotypic differences between humans and animal models are notable but may reflect species differences or incomplete penetrance.

results.result: The manuscript discusses potential roles for EECs and gut neurons in immune regulation, noting that EECs express Toll-like receptors and receptors for microbial metabolites that can stimulate hormone secretion, and that murine models of gut neuron/glial defects and human gut neuron deficiency (Hirschsprung's disease) are associated with colitis.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 provide literature context supported by appropriate citations (Bogunovic et al., 2007; Lebrun et al., 2017; Palazzo et al., 2007; Selleri et al., 2008; Bush et al., 1998; Cheng et al., 2010; Fujimoto et al., 1988; Demehri et al., 2013; Gosain, 2016; Gosain and Brinkman, 2015). This background supports the biological plausibility of the findings.

results.result: The manuscript concludes that the ultra-rare SCGN p.R77H variant causes Mendelian early-onset ulcerative colitis, that functional deficiency in SCGN can result in intestinal inflammation, and that this implicates the neuroendocrine cellular compartment in IBD.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C9, and C10 represent the main conclusions. While the genetic, cellular, and mouse data are strong, establishing causality for a Mendelian disease typically requires: (1) multiple unrelated families with the same phenotype and gene, (2) functional rescue experiments in patient cells, or (3) engineered models recapitulating the exact variant. The study presents one family, and while the mouse knockout and cellular models support loss of function, the specific R77H variant's effects are only tested in cell culture and zebrafish. The conclusion that this variant "causes" disease is strongly supported but not definitively proven by current standards. Additional families or patient-derived cell rescue experiments would strengthen causality claims.
